# Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a General Multi-Robot Planner for One Warehouse

University of Southern California    Han Zhang
Affiliation: Symbotic{yimintan,biyik}@usc.edu, svenk@uci.edu,
{hanzhang,shchan,jichen}@symbotic.com    Shao-Hung Chan

{hanzhang,shchan,jichen}@symbotic.com    Erdem Bıyık Affiliation: Thomas

###### Abstract

No algorithm is best on all problems, but a real warehouse is a narrow
problem: its layout and processes rarely change. Operators still run one
general multi-robot planner at many sites, because experts cannot tune
it for each one. In this work, which we call Late Autumn, we explore
whether LLM coding agents running autonomous research can _specialize_ a
general planner for one site, trading generality for throughput, much as
post-training adapts a pretrained LLM to one task. We study six
campaigns on a lifelong planner that combines task assignment with
multi-agent path finding, on a floor modeled on an existing automated
warehouse. We find that (1) the agents raise throughput by 22–60%, and
the gains hold on unseen seeds; (2) they rediscover known MAPF
mechanisms, such as corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and
rollouts, and independent campaigns find the same bottleneck; (3) the
gains largely carry over to another layout, a larger fleet, and other
service times, shrink with a smaller fleet, and mostly vanish under an
outbound-heavy demand mix; and (4) each final patch (0.7k–2.4k lines) is
a chain of scored commits with a median step of 27 lines, so experts can
review it, and review finds problems that the score misses; some patches
multiply planner compute by over 100$`\times`$. LLM agents can therefore
turn each site’s bias into extra throughput at little engineering cost,
with reviewable patches; we expect experts to shift toward designing
insightful metrics and fast simulators that mirror the real problem.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2611.02391v1/robots.png)

Figure 1: Commercial warehouse robot systems.

Automated warehouses move goods with fleets of robots that shuttle cases
between storage aisles and stations. Commercial systems take many forms
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")):
drive units that carry shelves to pickers (Amazon Robotics, Geek+), bots
that carry cases through multi-level aisles (Symbotic), robots on a grid
above stacked bins (AutoStore), rack-climbing tote robots (Hai
Robotics), and robots that work beside human pickers (Locus Robotics).
The coordination layer must repeatedly assign tasks to robots and plan
collision-free paths for all of them, a lifelong variant of Multi-Agent
Path Finding (MAPF) with target assignment ([Ma et al.,
2017](#bib.bib21); [Li et al., 2021](#bib.bib17); [Ma and Koenig,
2016](#bib.bib20)). MAPF is NP-hard to solve optimally ([Yu and LaValle,
2013](#bib.bib37)), so large fleets call for fast suboptimal planners
such as PIBT ([Okumura et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)) and LaCAM ([Okumura,
2023b](#bib.bib24)). We use a lifelong version of ITA-LaCAM ([Tang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)), which couples target assignment with LaCAM
search. As a concrete example, we model the floor of one existing
automated warehouse; since MAPF models any AGV warehouse as a graph with
tasks, the approach is not tied to it.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(a\) auto-research loop

![Refer to caption](2611.02391v1/map_tuned.png)

\(b\) tuned site

Figure 2: (a) The agent edits a general planner for one site, self-tests
on public seeds with traces, and is scored only on hidden seeds; experts
review the diffs. (b) The tuned site: aisles and station lanes are
one-wide corridors, and one cell links the two halves.

This planner is a _general_ algorithm, designed for a broad class of
layouts and workloads. By the No Free Lunch theorems, averaged over all
possible problems, every search algorithm performs equally
well ([Wolpert and Macready, 1997](#bib.bib35)). Real sites are far from
this average: warehouses differ in aisle geometry, fleet size, carry
capacity, demand mix, and service times, but each one runs the same
layout and largely fixed processes every day. A planner can therefore
trade generality that one site never needs for throughput, much as
post-training specializes a pretrained LLM. Until now, only experts
could exploit this bias, by inspecting traces and changing cost or
priority rules, and no company can do this for its growing number of
sites. An agent that can would give each site extra throughput at almost
no engineering cost.

LLM-based coding agents now perform parts of this loop ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22); [Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), but most of this
evidence comes from short programs with cheap, deterministic scores. A
warehouse planner differs in three ways. First, the agent edits a
complete planner (assignment, search, and simulation) rather than a
single heuristic function. Second, the score comes from a stochastic
simulation in which many changes are smaller than the noise, so an agent
can “improve” by chance. Third, a change reaches physical robots only
after an engineer understands it and trusts it. We therefore ask:

1.  RQ1
    After autonomous research on one site configuration, does the
    planner’s throughput really improve?
2.  RQ2
    What methods do the agents propose?
3.  RQ3
    Are these methods site-specific, or do they work for other warehouse
    configurations?
4.  RQ4
    How large is each improving change, and can an expert review it to
    confirm, from first principles, that it is correct?

In this work, which we call Late Autumn, we explore this idea with an
existing auto-research system and answer these questions with a case
study. An agent receives the planner repository and a task contract that
fixes one site configuration. It may change any planner logic, but it is
scored only on hidden seeds by an isolated host, and it must commit and
evaluate every candidate. We ran six campaigns (three model families,
three knowledge settings; 600 official evaluations), re-evaluated each
best patch on fresh seeds and on seven held-out configurations, and
analyzed every diff that raised the best score. Our results show that
every campaign’s best patch beats the baseline on all 20 fresh seeds, by
22–63%, and that the patches keep a significant gain in 40 of 42
held-out configurations. Our contributions are:

1.  1.  A case study of agent-driven specialization of a lifelong MAPF
        planner to one site, run with hidden-seed scoring, a mandatory
        commit-and-evaluate lifecycle, and compute accounting.
2.  2.  Evidence that agents raise throughput by 22–60% (RQ1).
3.  3.  A catalog of the discovered mechanisms (RQ2), a transfer study
        (RQ3), and a code-level analysis (RQ4): improving steps are small
        (median 27 lines), so even the final patches can be reviewed commit
        by commit, and review finds problems that the score misses.

## 2 Problem Definition and Baseline

#### Lifelong TAPF with multi-carry robots.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a 4-connected grid graph whose vertices are free
cells; self-loops represent waiting. Agents $`I=\{1,\dots,N\}`$ start at
distinct vertices and each can carry at most $`K`$ tasks. Tasks are
released online; a task $`\tau=(s_{\tau},G_{\tau})`$ has a pickup vertex
$`s_{\tau}`$ and a goal set $`G_{\tau}\subseteq V`$, any vertex of which
completes the delivery. Let $`x_{i}(t)\in V`$ be the location of agent
$`i`$ at timestep $`t`$. A plan is valid if, for all agents $`i\neq j`$
and timesteps $`t`$: 1) $`x_{i}(t{+}1){=}x_{i}(t)`$ or
$`(x_{i}(t),x_{i}(t{+}1))\in E`$; 2) $`x_{i}(t)\neq x_{j}(t)`$ (no
vertex conflict); 3) agents never swap vertices (no edge conflict); and
4) agent $`i`$ picks up $`\tau`$ only by staying at $`s_{\tau}`$ for
$`d_{p}`$ consecutive timesteps while it carries fewer than $`K`$ tasks,
and delivers $`\tau`$ only by staying at some $`g\in G_{\tau}`$ for
$`d_{d}`$ timesteps. The objective is _throughput_: tasks completed
within horizon $`H`$, divided by $`H`$. Each planner call has a 1 s
wall-clock limit.

#### Baseline planner.

Our planner, a lifelong version of ITA-LaCAM ([Tang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib34)), replans after every pickup or delivery or when its
plan runs out. A Hungarian matching assigns each agent one goal option
(a pickup, a goal cell of a carried case, or a costly wait), costed by
distance plus service time, with at most one agent per pickup or drop
cell; as in ITA-CBS ([Tang et al., 2023](#bib.bib32)), the matching is
repaired incrementally at each search node. LaCAM ([Okumura,
2023b](#bib.bib24)) with FOCAL node selection then generates
configurations with PIBT ([Okumura et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)) until some
agent completes a service. The planner has 9.0k lines of C++ and needs
4.8 ms per call at the tuned site
(§[4](#S4 "4 Auto-Research Setup ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")):
its anytime refinement exits after the first solution (the stopping test
compares quantities on different scales), so over 99% of the budget is
unused. It reaches a hidden-seed throughput of 1.23 (pseudo-code in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Baseline Planner Pseudo-Code ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")).

## 3 Related Work

#### MAPF in warehouses.

PIBT and LaCAM plan for hundreds of agents in milliseconds ([Okumura
et al., 2022](#bib.bib25); [Okumura, 2023b](#bib.bib24); [Okumura,
2023a](#bib.bib23)), unlike optimal CBS ([Sharon et al.,
2015](#bib.bib29); [Stern et al., 2019](#bib.bib30)). TAPF couples
target assignment with path finding ([Ma and Koenig, 2016](#bib.bib20);
[Hönig et al., 2018](#bib.bib8); [Tang et al., 2023](#bib.bib32); [Tang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Kumagai and Okumura, 2026](#bib.bib15)), and
lifelong variants model warehouses with continuous task arrival ([Ma
et al., 2017](#bib.bib21); [Li et al., 2021](#bib.bib17); [Chan et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib5)). Guidance-graph optimization ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39); [Zang et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)) and imitation
learning ([Jiang et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) raise throughput; learned
planners and fleet foundation models serve many maps ([Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Agaskar et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). These methods are
designed by researchers for a class of instances; we study whether an
agent can do the remaining site-specific engineering.

#### LLM agents for algorithm engineering.

LLM-driven program search discovered new constructions and
heuristics ([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22); [Lange et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18); [Ye et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)), agentic systems run
research loops over code ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19); [Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), and benchmarks
evaluate them ([Chan et al., 2024a](#bib.bib4); [Huang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9); [Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Press et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26); [Imajuku et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). There, programs
are small and scores are cheap. LLMs fail when they plan MAPF paths
directly ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)); we let them _write planner
code_ instead, so the planner remains a verifiable search algorithm.

## 4 Auto-Research Setup

In this section, we describe the auto-research setup: the agent’s tools,
the task contract it must follow, and how we re-evaluate its results. We
use CORAL ([Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)) to run one autonomous coding
agent per campaign in its own git worktree
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")a).
The agent can read and edit all code, build, test, inspect traces, and
request evaluations. A natural-language _task contract_
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Task Contract Excerpt ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse"))
sets the rules below.

#### Site and workload.

The site the agents tune
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")b)
follows one existing warehouse floor: a $`35{\times}39`$ grid with 691
free cells, 19 one-wide storage aisles of 20 cells, and 8 one-wide
station lanes; a wall splits it into two halves joined by a single cell.
An _outbound_ task (probability $`p_{\text{out}}{=}0.5`$) starts at a
storage cell and may be delivered to any of 3 cells of one station lane;
an _inbound_ task starts at a station cell and may be delivered to any
of 3 storage cells. New tasks are released so that $`2N`$ tasks stay
unfinished, which keeps the system saturated. We use $`N{=}100`$,
$`K{=}2`$, $`H{=}400`$, and $`d_{p}{=}d_{d}{=}4`$.

#### Fixed site, free algorithm.

The contract fixes this site and workload. The agent may change any
planner, assignment, or goal-selection logic and any algorithm-side
default. It may not modify the map, the task process, or the benchmark
runner (the evaluation host overwrites them), hard-code seeds or
map-specific shortcuts, or fabricate outputs; the grader recomputes
throughput from the completed tasks.

#### Isolated evaluation.

Throughput depends on how much search fits into 1 s, so builds and
benchmarks run on a separate host with pinned 10-core slots. A
_self-test_ runs public seeds 0–9 and returns per-seed traces. An
_official evaluation_ runs 10 hidden seeds and returns only aggregates.
The same binary is reproducible on one slot, but contention can move the
10-seed mean by about 0.025; six evaluations of the unmodified baseline
spanned 1.198–1.249. The contract therefore treats mean changes below
0.03 as noise.

#### Commit-and-evaluate lifecycle.

Every candidate that changes behavior, builds, and yields valid output
must be committed and officially evaluated _before_ the agent keeps,
reverts, or abandons it. This rule prevents silent cherry-picking and
gives us the complete record. CORAL adds periodic prompts to _reflect_
(every 2 evaluations), _consolidate_ (every 8), and _pivot_ (on
plateaus). A campaign stops after 100 official evaluations.

#### Safety property.

The simulator validates every executed joint move for vertex and edge
conflicts. As long as a patch leaves this validator unchanged, which
review confirmed for all 102 new-best steps, a patch can lower
throughput but cannot produce a collision in an executed plan.

#### Knowledge settings and campaigns.

In the _paper-grounded_ setting, every idea must cite one of 137 briefs
of MAPF-related papers and competition reports. In the _open_ setting,
any source is allowed and must be named; _open+web_ also enables web
search. We ran six campaigns from the same commit at high reasoning
effort, with four models in three agent harnesses
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")).

#### Re-evaluation and transfer.

A campaign’s best hidden score is a maximum over noisy evaluations. We
therefore rebuilt the baseline and each best commit and ran them on 20
fresh seeds for the tuned site and for seven held-out configurations,
each changing one factor: an alternative layout
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Held-Out Layout ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")),
60 or 150 robots, $`K{=}1`$, an 80/20 outbound/inbound mix, and service
durations of 2 or 8, a total of 1,120 episodes (7 builds, 8
configurations, 20 seeds). _Gain_ is the paired throughput difference to
the baseline on the same seeds, with a 95% CI over seeds; a _new-best
step_ is an official evaluation that raises a campaign’s best hidden
score; its _size_ is the number of changed lines of algorithm code,
excluding tests, tools, and build files. All builds use GCC 10.5 -O3;
the re-evaluation runs used a 32-core AMD EPYC 9R14 host with 64 GB RAM.

### 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve?

![Refer to caption](2611.02391v1/trajectory.png)

Figure 3: (a) Best-so-far hidden-seed throughput (dots: single
evaluations, those below 1.0 on the bottom edge; gray band: six baseline
evaluations). (b) Size of the best commit so far (changed lines of
algorithm code); it drops when a new best comes from a branch with less
code. Solid: paper-grounded; dashed: open.

Figure 4: (a) Hidden-score gain per campaign by mechanism group; each
new-best step counts toward its main change, and retunes toward the
mechanism they tune. (b) Size of each new-best step versus its
increment; filled marks exceed the 0.03 noise floor. Sizes count
algorithm code only.

#### Yes, by 22–60%.

Every campaign raised hidden-seed throughput far beyond the noise floor
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse"),
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")).
The best campaign (Opus, paper-grounded) reached 1.973 tasks per
timestep, 60% above the baseline mean of 1.230. The four Claude-family
campaigns gained 43–60%, and both GPT campaigns plateaued near 1.50
(+22%).

#### The gains hold on fresh seeds.

On 20 seeds that no agent had seen, every best patch scores within
0.001–0.024 of its hidden best
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")),
so selection bias is small, and beats the baseline on all 20 seeds; for
example, the Opus/paper patch reaches 1.968 (+63%).

#### Gains come early, partly from compute.

The Claude-family campaigns reached 65–86% of their final gain within 20
evaluations (0.6–1.9 hours); only 27 of the 102 new-best steps exceed
the 0.03 noise floor. Relative to their baseline evaluation, the
paper-grounded Claude patches use 4–10$`\times`$ more planner time and
the open-setting patches 53–91$`\times`$ (mean calls of 0.3–0.6 s
against the 1 s limit). GPT-6.1 Sol’s last new best (+0.008) raised its
planner time 87-fold (112$`\times`$ its baseline).

### 5.2 RQ2: What did the agents propose?

We read all 102 diffs that raised the best score, together with the
agents’ notes
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Gains come early, partly from compute. ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse"),
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")a).

#### Independent campaigns found the same bottleneck.

On this floor, 470 of the 691 free cells lie in one-wide corridors, and
a servicing robot blocks everyone behind it. Three Claude campaigns
found this, from traces (“corridor entrances are occupied 89% of the
time”) or from a cited paper, and converged on two rules. A
_corridor-exit priority_ gives a PIBT priority boost to a robot inside a
corridor whose goal lies outside it, so that priority inheritance pushes
entering robots back instead of pushing the leaving robot deeper (+0.09
to +0.14; cf. PIBTTP ([Fujitani et al., 2022](#bib.bib7))). A
_corridor-blocking cost_ makes pickup and drop cells behind occupied
corridor cells more expensive in the matching (+0.12 to +0.28; cf.
idle-time-aware assignment ([Kou et al., 2019](#bib.bib14))). All three
detected corridors generically, as components of degree-2 vertices.
These rules provide 28–67% of those campaigns’ gains.

#### Agents spent the idle budget.

Agents ported local guidance ([Arita and Okumura, 2025](#bib.bib2);
[Arita and Okumura, 2026](#bib.bib3)) (+0.35 in Opus/paper), added
flow-dependent edge weights ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib39); [Zang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)) (+0.13 in Fable/paper), and built rollout
planners; Fable/open+web replaced LaCAM’s search with the best of many
noisy PIBT rollouts (+0.38 in one step).

#### Sources and failures.

Paper-grounded campaigns cited a brief in 97–99% of evaluations but used
only 18–44 of 137 briefs; 79% of Opus/open candidates came from its own
diagnosis; the web was never used. Comparing lineages, we find two
reasons why the GPT campaigns plateaued near 1.50. First, they turned to
the library instead of the traces and never built corridor rules for the
aisles; the same local-guidance paper gave Opus +0.24 but GPT 0.98–1.30,
because GPT used a 5-step window and no warm start. Second, they
followed CORAL’s “hardest idea, three evaluations” prompt literally,
with median attempts of 66 and 290 added lines (Claude: 4–16).

### 5.3 RQ3: Specific or general?

![Refer to caption](2611.02391v1/transfer.png)

Figure 5: Paired gain (%) of each unchanged best patch over the
baseline, 20 fresh seeds per cell; all 95% CIs exclude zero. Bottom row:
baseline throughput.

#### Code-level generality.

We graded each frontier step as G0 (generic features only), G1 (generic
code, layout-tuned constants), or G2 (scenario facts). Of 77
Claude-family steps, 12 are G0, 59 G1, and 6 G2; none hard-codes seeds,
coordinates, or the map.

#### Transfer.

Applied unchanged to seven held-out configurations
(Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.3 RQ3: Specific or general? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")),
the patches gain significantly in 40 of 42 cells. On the alternative
layout, the patches keep 57–91% of their absolute gain, because its
aisles are still one-wide. We observe a clear trend with congestion:
with 60 robots only 25–43% of the absolute gain remains, whereas with
150 robots 64–110% remains. This is because the discovered mechanisms
target blocking in one-wide corridors, which grows with fleet size.
Relative gains also stay close to the tuned ones for single-carry robots
and service durations of 2 and 8. The exception is the 80/20
outbound-heavy mix, which sends most deliveries to the 8 station lanes:
the Claude patches keep only +3 to +10%, and both GPT patches _lose_ 6%.
Site-specific campaigns thus produced mostly general improvements, but a
new demand mix calls for a new campaign.

### 5.4 RQ4: How large are the changes, and can humans review them?

#### Steps and patches are small.

The median improving step changes 27 lines, 27 of the 102 steps only
retune a constant, and the largest gains came from 36–383-line
mechanisms
(Figures [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")b,
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Does throughput really improve? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")b;
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Example of an Improving Step ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")).
The final patches (0.7k–1.5k lines for Claude, 1.3k–2.4k for GPT) are
modest next to the 9k-line planner, and each is a chain of 13–49
officially scored commits (median 4–51 lines) that an expert can review
one at a time; this also exposes dead code (26% of the lines added by
Opus/paper).

#### Review is feasible and necessary.

Of the 24 frontier steps of Opus/paper, 7 are constant retunes, 10 are
local cost or priority rules that an expert can verify from first
principles, and 7 need careful review. Review found problems that the
score cannot reveal: (i) the Opus/open rollout stops at 880 ms and then
starts the main solve with a _fresh_ 1 s deadline, so the per-call limit
holds only empirically; (ii) a Monte-Carlo step redraws PIBT’s random
tie-breaks, so the executed configuration can differ from the scored
one; and (iii) dwell-sized constants and $`K{=}2`$ formulas are
hard-coded.

## 6 Lessons and Conclusion

LLM agents can specialize a general algorithm to one site for extra
performance: campaigns raised throughput by 22–60% with trace-diagnosed
corridor rules and with guidance and rollouts that use idle compute, and
the gains mostly transferred. As a site’s layout and processes rarely
change, this turns site bias into nearly free throughput and lower
logistics costs. The final patches can be reviewed commit by commit.
Since agents optimize exactly what the score and simulator measure, we
expect experts to shift from hand-tuning algorithms toward designing
insightful metrics and fast simulators that mirror the real problem. We
recommend short campaigns (about 20 evaluations), unseen-seed checks,
and a graded call-time limit. Next, we plan to deploy reviewed patches
on physical robots.

## Limitations

This is a case study of one planner and one family of sites. All results
come from simulation; we have not yet deployed an agent-generated patch
on physical robots. We ran one campaign per (model, harness, knowledge
setting) combination, so differences between campaigns combine the
effects of the model, the agent harness (Claude Code, Kiro, Codex), the
knowledge setting, and run-to-run variance; the comparison is
indicative, not causal. The best hidden score of each campaign is
selected from up to 100 noisy evaluations and is therefore optimistic;
we report fresh-seed re-evaluations to correct for this. Our
reviewability analysis is based on diff statistics and on an
LLM-assisted code reading whose key findings we checked against the
source. Finally, the agents optimized throughput only. They could trade
other operational metrics, such as task latency, energy use, or robot
wear, which we did not measure.

## Ethical Considerations

Agent-generated changes to software that controls physical robots carry
safety risk. In our protocol, agents never act on hardware; they edit
planner code that is scored in simulation, and the planner’s collision
checks remain the final safety layer. We argue that every patch should
pass expert review and staged testing before deployment. The intended
use is to let a small engineering team support many sites; this may
change the work of operations engineers, and we recommend keeping humans
responsible for deployment decisions. Higher throughput from the same
robots can lower the cost of warehouse logistics for operators and their
customers; this benefit should be weighed against the extra planner
compute that some patches need. No personal data was used.

## Appendix C Task Contract Excerpt

The contract was given to the agents in Chinese; we translate its key
rules. _“You may generally change planner, assignment, or goal-candidate
behavior. You may not change the fixed official target, hard-code
seed/task/map shortcuts, fabricate CSV, trace, or schedule outputs, or
optimize only the output format.”_ _“A mean change smaller than 0.03 on
public seeds is not a signal; prefer trace-derived behavior signals.”_
_“Once a behavior-changing candidate is finalized, builds, and produces
valid output, you must commit it and run an official evaluation, whether
your self-test shows improvement, no change, or regression.”_
_“Iteration time is also a resource … only accept a clearly higher
runtime cost when the throughput evidence is strong (about 0.1 or
more).”_

## Appendix E Example of an Improving Step

Figure [8](#A5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix E Example of an Improving Step ‣ Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a GeneralMulti-Robot Planner for One Warehouse")
shows the C++ code added by the second evaluation of the Opus/open
campaign (commit 3400f25f): corridor detection and the corridor-exit
priority. The step adds 45 lines of algorithm code, removes 2, and
raised the hidden score from 1.238 to 1.380. A reviewer can check its
two claims, that corridors are connected components of vertices with
degree at most 2 and that only unsatisfied agents whose goal lies
outside their corridor are boosted, directly from the code.

```ltx_verbatim
// (in the TAPFPlanner constructor)
auto next_component = 0;
for (auto v : ins->G.V) {
  if (v->neighbor.size() > 2 || corridor_component[v->id] >= 0) continue;
  auto stack = std::vector<Vertex*>{v};
  corridor_component[v->id] = next_component;
  while (!stack.empty()) {
    auto u = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
    for (auto w : u->neighbor) {
      if (w->neighbor.size() > 2 || corridor_component[w->id] >= 0) continue;
      corridor_component[w->id] = next_component; stack.push_back(w);
    }
  }
  ++next_component;
}
// (at the LaCAM root)
// An agent inside a single-lane corridor whose goal lies outside it is
// leaving; give it precedence so agents entering the corridor do not push
// it deeper.
constexpr float kCorridorExitPriority = 10.0f;
auto boosted = false;
for (auto i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
  if (S_init->satisfied[i] || S_init->service_assignment[i] >= 0) continue;
  const auto comp = corridor_component[S_init->C[i]->id];
  if (comp < 0) continue;
  const auto goal = assigned_goal(S_init->assignment, i);
  if (goal == nullptr || corridor_component[goal->id] == comp) continue;
  S_init->priorities[i] += kCorridorExitPriority; boosted = true;
}
if (boosted) {
  std::sort(S_init->order.begin(), S_init->order.end(), [&](int a, int b) {
    return S_init->priorities[a] > S_init->priorities[b]; });
}
```

Figure 8: An agent-written improving step (corridor-exit priority,
+0.142 hidden throughput), from the diff of commit 3400f25f. Code and
comments are verbatim; we merged some short lines, dropped enclosing
braces, and added the two location notes in parentheses.
